title: The Ed Department's Meme Machine
author: Chad Aldeman
summary: Chad Aldeman uses the week of the elections to criticize the U.S. Department of Education's official Twitter account. His complaint is that an agency account paid for by taxpayers mixes serious, topical posts with AI-generated slop, fawning praise for the president and culture-war memes. He cites examples including cartoon characters such as Scooby-Doo and Elmo placed in political messaging, a series of 'Parents Know Best' ads that do not always get the facts right, and regular Friday posts of the president. He also points to the 'Making College Football Great Again' images that appeared after a Texas political controversy and never explain what the department wants fixed. His closing standard is that a public agency should explain its policies and how they help students and schools, working for everyone rather than a narrow partisan audience.
points: Aldeman separates legitimate agency communication, such as promoting policies and sharing useful information, from posts that read like campaign content on an official feed.
AI-generated images that borrow beloved cartoon characters for political messages feel inappropriate and raise unresolved copyright questions.
Regular posts praising the president read as over-the-top flattery rather than substantive communication about the department's work.
The 'Making College Football Great Again' posts never say whether the concern is head injuries, name-image-likeness deals or sports gambling, which leaves their purpose unclear.
The underlying test he applies is whether a public servant's output serves all citizens, and he finds the account instead has a much narrower audience in mind.
quotes: Because it’s an official government account that should be doing serious business.
But sprinkled between those, they put out a steady stream of AI-generated slop, fawning praise for the president, and culture-war memes.
An official agency account should help people understand what the department is doing, but a lot of the posts leave me wondering who, exactly, the department thinks it’s working for.
But using beloved cartoon characters to carry a government message feels wrong.

This type of thing would be normal for a campaign account. But on the Department of Education’s official feed, it reads as over-the-top praise for a figurehead more than any substantive communication about the department’s work.
The timing could be a coincidence, but the posts never explain what the department thinks needs fixing about college football.

It’s fair game for the Department of Education to use its social media accounts to promote their policies, share useful information, or explain how what they are doing is helping students and schools.
But as public servants, they should be working for all of us. Instead, they often veer into partisan meme territory and seem to have a much narrower audience in mind.
